country.name: Iran
country.tagline: Neolithic resinated wine in the Zagros and the wine poetry of Hafez; production banned since 1979.

stats.note: OIV 2025: 128 kha of vines, all for table grapes and raisins (Iran is a major raisin producer). Commercial wine production has been illegal since the 1979 revolution; licensed religious minorities may make wine for their own use.

country.overview:
Iran holds some of the oldest evidence of wine in the world. At Hajji Firuz Tepe, a Neolithic village in the Zagros mountains south of Lake Urmia excavated by the Penn Museum in 1958 to 1968, six jars of about nine litres each, set into the floor of a mudbrick house of about 5400 to 5000 BC, held residues of tartaric acid and terebinth resin: a resinated wine, published by Patrick McGovern in Nature in 1996 and for two decades the oldest chemical evidence of grape wine. At Godin Tepe, further south, jars of about 3100 to 2900 BC with red residue and wine stains on their sides (they were stored lying down) show a trade in wine along the routes to Mesopotamia.

Persian kings feasted on wine at Persepolis, and wine remained central to court culture and poetry after Islam. The ghazals of Hafez of Shiraz (fourteenth century) and the quatrains attributed to Omar Khayyam made wine the great metaphor of mystical love, and Shiraz, in Fars province, was renowned for its wine into the twentieth century; European travellers such as Jean Chardin described it in the seventeenth. The Syrah grape is sometimes said to come from Shiraz, but DNA has shown it is a cross of two French varieties from the Rhône. Before 1979 Iran had a few hundred wineries; after the revolution commercial alcohol was banned, and Iran's vineyards today grow table grapes and raisins (Takestan near Qazvin and Malayer are major raisin centres).

history.title: Hajji Firuz Tepe
history.text: Neolithic jars sunk in a house floor held tartaric acid and terebinth resin: resinated wine (McGovern et al., Nature 1996).

history.title: Godin Tepe
history.text: Jars with wine residues and evidence of storage on their sides at a trading post on the route to Mesopotamia.

history.title: Persepolis
history.text: Achaemenid administrative tablets at Persepolis record wine rations for workers and the court.

history.title: Hafez of Shiraz
history.text: The poet Hafez made wine the central image of Persian mystical poetry; his tomb in Shiraz is a place of pilgrimage.

history.title: Prohibition
history.text: After the Islamic Revolution commercial wine production was banned.

country.climate_soils: High plateaus and Zagros valleys with hot, dry summers and cold winters; irrigated vineyards for table grapes and raisins.
further_reading: The Pursuit of Pleasure: Drugs and Stimulants in Iranian History, Rudi Matthee

sites.name: Hajji Firuz Tepe
sites.text: A Neolithic mound in the Gadar valley south of Lake Urmia where six jars of about 5400 to 5000 BC, set in a kitchen floor, held tartaric acid and terebinth resin, the first chemical proof of ancient resinated wine (published 1996).

sites.name: Godin Tepe
sites.text: Late Uruk-period trading post in the central Zagros (about 3100 to 2900 BC) whose jars held wine and were stored lying on their sides.

sites.name: Tomb of Hafez, Shiraz
sites.text: The garden tomb of the fourteenth-century poet whose ghazals made wine the central metaphor of Persian poetry, in the city once famous for its wine.

sites.name: Persepolis
sites.text: Achaemenid ceremonial capital (UNESCO) whose administrative tablets record wine rations; reliefs show tribute bearers with vessels.
